A solute that biodegrades or transforms loses dissolved mass at a rate proportional to its concentration: $\partial C/\partial t = -\lambda C$, with decay constant $\lambda$ [1/T] and half-life $t_{1/2} = \ln 2 / \lambda$. Decay **lowers the peak and the plateau** (for a continuous source, the steady concentration at the well) but — unlike sorption — does **not** delay the front. Two of the case-study contaminants decay: **benzene** (group 2, aerobic biodegradation, $t_{1/2}\approx139$ d) and **ammonium** (group 7, nitrification, $t_{1/2}\approx35$ d).

**Why.** It is *not* simply that the transverse grid Péclet is large. On a grid **aligned** with the flow, MODFLOW 6's TVD scheme adds essentially **no** transverse numerical dispersion, so a high $Pe_T$ *by itself* does **not** doom the lateral width ([04t](04t_model_implementation.ipynb) verifies this directly against the 2D analytical solution). The lateral claim fails for two *other* reasons near a doublet: (a) the flow is **convergent and oblique to the grid**, which *does* produce real cross-wind numerical dispersion, and (b) the physical plume is **sub-cell** ($\alpha_T = 1$ m, narrower than even the refined ~10 m cells), so no feasible grid can *represent* it. So restrict every threshold claim to the **flow axis / receptors**; for the genuine **lateral / wellfield-protection** question, don't read it off the smeared concentration field — use **particle tracking** (a capture zone), which is advective and free of the cross-wind artefact ([08t](08t_model_application.ipynb) Rung D).

**Parameters and their identifiability.** The transport unknowns are longitudinal dispersivity $\alpha_L$, effective porosity $\phi_e$, retardation $R$, and first-order decay $\lambda$. The catch is the **$\phi_e$–$\alpha_L$ trade-off**: *both* reshape a single breakthrough curve — a lower $\phi_e$ shifts arrival earlier (faster mean water velocity), while a larger $\alpha_L$ spreads the pulse and advances its leading toe — so one BTC alone cannot separate them. A **tracer test breaks the trade-off** by moment analysis: the mean arrival time $\bar{t}$ fixes the mean water velocity $u = x/\bar{t}$, and since $\phi_e = q/u$ (with $q$ the Darcy flux from the calibrated flow model), porosity is determined **independently**. With $\phi_e$ pinned, only $\alpha_L$ is left — a 1-D fit to the curve's spread. This is the transport analogue of the flow track's pumping-test constraint (05f): an independent measurement collapses a non-unique calibration to a single-parameter search.

**Data you'd need.** Observed **breakthrough curve(s)** — solute concentration vs. time at the monitoring / extraction well — and/or a dedicated **tracer-test BTC**. **Two numbers that are *not* the answer, and why.** (i) The **capture fraction ≈0.49** is a property of the **probe disc**, not of the doublet — it is "the fraction of a 120 m disc that happens to lie inside the capture zone". That disc even reaches ~30 m *downgradient* of the well, and those points can never be captured yet are counted as "escaped". Read the captured/escaped **scatter**; the scalar is an artefact of where we chose to release. (ii) The **maximum captured offset** (printed above) is a sampling statistic and a *lower bound*: in an unchanged flow field it grows with the probe radius, and the point that sets it sits *upgradient* of the spill, not on the spill transect. Neither is a capture-zone half-width. (Note also that 199, not 200, particles are released: one release point landed inside the extraction-well cell and was dropped, since such a particle would report a travel time of exactly 0 d. That dropped point *would* have been captured, so dropping it slightly **deflates** the fraction to ≈0.49.)

**How the advection engine is verified.** Not against the ADE's day-39 peak — PRT's advective timescale (~20 d) and a concentration peak are different quantities, and no simple identity connects them in a converging 2-D field. Instead, PRT is checked against **the flow field it was handed**: integrating the mean water velocity $u = q/\phi_e$ straight from the GWF budget (`DATA-SPDIS`, locked porosity 0.20) along the spill→well axis gives a path-averaged **4.25 m/d**, and PRT's particles report a path-averaged **4.15 m/d** (median arc length 84.4 m in ≈20 d) — agreement to ~2%, from two independent computations, with nothing tuned. Honest limit: PRT and the ADE share the **same flow field, grid and porosity** — only the transport engines differ — so this check verifies the *particle tracker*, and cannot detect an error in the *flow solution*.
